messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ibrahim had spent nearly forty years around explosives, and it was that expertise that made the day of the chemical exposure feel so incomprehensible. He was working as a bomb disposal technician, moving through a secured industrial site in heavy protective gear, when a ruptured container released a toxic chemical cloud into the work area. The alarm went up, men shouted, and the sharp sting of the air made his throat burn before he could get fully clear. He remembered the metallic echo of voices through the mask, the rush of boots on concrete, and later the antiseptic smell of the emergency department as he was checked over and decontaminated. Since then, those same sensory fragments had become dangerous in their own right. A loud bang from a cart in the corridor, the smell of disinfectant at a clinic, or even walking into his own workplace now pulled him back into the moment of exposure with a force that felt immediate and bodily, as if the danger were already in the room again.

In the months that followed, Ibrahim began organizing his life around the expectation of threat. He was constantly scanning his surroundings for signs of danger, reading doorways, windows, parked vehicles, and the spacing between people with a vigilance that never fully switched off. He always identified escape routes before he felt comfortable anywhere, whether he was sitting in a staff meeting, entering a restaurant, or waiting in the hallway outside an appointment. If someone touched him unexpectedly, he reacted with alarm, his body jerking before he could stop it, embarrassed by how quickly he went from composed to braced for impact. He had come to believe that if he was not watching carefully enough, if he failed to anticipate where he could get out, something terrible could happen again without warning. Even the workplace that had once given him confidence now fed that fear: every time he returned to it, the routines of the job and the industrial surroundings brought the exposure back to mind, and that renewed his certainty that danger could arrive anywhere, without a clear signal.

Those same triggers also shaped what he began to do to keep himself steady. Ibrahim started avoiding being alone in a room or building, telling himself that solitary spaces made it too easy for his mind to drift back to the chemical release and the hospital. He avoided hospitals, ambulances, and physical examinations, refusing routine care whenever he could and making excuses if the appointment sounded even slightly invasive. At the same time, he began working excessively, taking on extra shifts and lingering at the depot long after tasks were finished because staying busy was the only way he knew to keep from being alone with his thoughts. The strategy helped briefly, but it also left him exhausted and more keyed up by the end of the day, and that exhaustion made the world feel even less manageable. The more he used work and constant company to stay away from quiet moments, the more he arrived home already tense, already watching, already convinced that he had to stay one step ahead.

Over time, that constant self-protection deepened the sense of danger rather than easing it. Because Ibrahim spent so much effort avoiding the places and moments that reminded him of the incident, he had fewer chances to feel settled in them again, and the alarms in his body stayed loud. He found himself scanning more intensely whenever he was alone, and the moment he heard a sudden noise or caught the antiseptic smell of a medical corridor, his whole attention narrowed to danger again. It was in those moments that his startle response felt most humiliating to him, and he became even more reluctant to go into hospitals or sit by himself in a quiet room where the sensations might catch him off guard. At work, a loud noise from equipment or a shouted instruction could set the same cycle in motion, leaving him jumpy, checking exits, and trying to outrun the feeling by burying himself in another task.

By the time he sought help, Ibrahim was 62, still married, and increasingly worried that the life he had built around control was shrinking. His wife had begun noticing how often he chose extra work over sitting at home, how carefully he positioned himself near doors, and how quickly he tensed when she touched his shoulder without warning. He came to treatment because he was tired of living as if every room needed an exit plan and every unfamiliar smell or sound might mean catastrophe. What frightened him most was the fear that he would never again feel safe enough to rest, and what he hoped for, more quietly, was to be able to sit in a room with his wife, hear a sudden sound, and not feel driven immediately back into danger.
